title: Modeling of Transformation Temperatures in Cast Martensitic Stainless Steels-CA6NM: Effects of Composition, Heating Rate, and Grain Size
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: ASTM A487 CA6NM is a cast martensitic stainless steel offering an excellent combination of strength, toughness, and corrosion resistance, making it widely used in marine, industrial, and energy applications (Ref  1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 ,  5 ,  6 - 7 ). However, its susceptibility to sulfide stress cracking in hydrogen sulfide service limits adoption in petroleum environments, necessitating strict hardness control, typically 22 HRC (Ref  1 ,  6 ,  8 ,  9 ). Achieving this requirement relies critically on precise tempering strategies (Ref  3 ,  10 ).

Critical temperatures are often estimated using thermodynamic software or from empirical formulas. While thermodynamic tools and empirical models exist, they generally neglect kinetic effects and exhibit poor predictive capability for low carbon—high-Ni martensitic stainless steels, like CA6NM (Ref  10 ,  15 ,  17 ,  18 ,  19 ,  20 - 21 ). Moreover, systematic experimental measurements of transformation behavior across the CA6NM composition space remain scarce. Empirical formula based on the effects of alloying elements, heating rates, and prior microstructures on the critical temperatures will provide accurate prediction of the critical temperatures for better heat treatment design.

sections.heading: Materials and Methods
paragraphs: In this work, commercial-grade martensitic stainless steel casting with ACI designation CA6NM (ASTM A487/A487M) was investigated. Six different cast materials from different foundries, designated F1-F6, were studied; five were received in the as-cast condition and one in the tempered condition. The six materials investigated were obtained from different foundries and were supplied in a range of initial conditions, including as-cast, tempered, and hot-rolled states, with both clean cast sections and runner/riser material represented. Metallographic examination of the as-cast conditions revealed localized micro-segregation, manifested as compositional variation and microstructural heterogeneity. Such segregation is expected to produce spatial variations in local alloy chemistry, which can, in turn, lead to non-uniform austenite formation behavior and increased scatter in measured critical transformation temperatures. To minimize the influence of this solidification-induced chemical inhomogeneity and establish a consistent microstructural baseline, all materials were normalized prior to evaluation. This treatment effectively reduced microstructural variability, allowing the measured transformation temperatures to be interpreted as intrinsic material responses rather than artifacts of as-cast segregation. Chemical compositions (Table  1 ) were measured using optical emission spectroscopy (OES; Oxford Instruments) for metallic elements and combustion analysis (LECO) for C, S, and N. Reported values represent averages of five measurements. To ensure consistent initial microstructures, specimens (~85 × 44 × 44 mm) were normalized at 1050 °C for 90 min and air-cooled. Microstructures were characterized by standard metallographic preparation, etched with Vilella’s reagent, and imaged by optical microscopy (Nikon Instruments).

Dilatometric experiments were conducted using a LINSEIS push-rod dilatometer on cylindrical specimens (ϕ3 × 10 mm), see Fig.  1 . Prior austenite grain size, heating rate and composition effects on transformation behavior were evaluated for all six CA6NM compositions at 0.1, 1, and 10 °C/s. Owing to the high hardenability of CA6NM, which results in fully martensitic microstructures even at extremely low cooling rates (Ref  5 ), the influence of cooling rate on critical temperatures was neglected. In addition, the study focuses on inter-critical transformation properties which are independent of cooling rates. Consequently, a constant cooling rate of 10 °C/s was applied across all measurements, and all specimens were air-cooled. Fig. 1 Dilatometric test: (a) image of the utilized dilatometer and (b) example of extracted transformation curve showing the Ac₁ and Ac₃ points by the tangent method

Grain size effects were investigated using F5 material subjected to austenitization at 1050 °C and 1150 °C for 10 min, 1 h, and 5 h, followed by water quenching. Samples were foil-wrapped with titanium getters to minimize oxidation and decarburization inside a box furnace. Grain size was measured manually using optical microscope and MATLAB subroutine. Subsequently, the effects of grain size on transformation temperatures were determined through dilatometric measurements.

sections.heading: Chemical Compositions
paragraphs: The chemical compositions of the CA6NM materials obtained from the six foundries after normalization treatment are summarized in Table  1 . While some of the measured elemental concentrations fall within the composition limits specified by ASTM A487/A487M for this alloy, minor deviations were observed in the silicon content of the F4 material and the chromium content of the F3 material. These compositions were at the upper and lower limits of the ASTM-specified ranges, respectively. Overall, the alloy chemistries examined in this study are representative of the compositional variability permitted for CA6NM within the ASTM A487/A487M specification.

paragraphs: Collectively, the widening gap between experimentally measured and equilibrium-predicted critical temperatures emphasizes the dominant role of transformation kinetics under non-equilibrium heating conditions and highlights the coupled effects of alloy chemistry and heating rate on austenite formation in cast martensitic stainless steels. These results indicate that predictive frameworks incorporating non-equilibrium transformation kinetics are necessary for the reliable design and control of heat treatment schedules in CA6NM and related cast martensitic stainless steels. Their use becomes particularly important under rapid heating conditions, such as induction heat treatment, where equilibrium-based assumptions can lead to systematic errors in critical transformation temperature selection.

sections.heading: Effects of Prior Austenite Grain Size (PAGs)
Model Validation and Statistical Assessment
paragraphs: Although the regression framework was developed using six nominal alloy chemistries, the calibration dataset consisted of multiple transformation measurements obtained over several heating rates and processing conditions, thereby providing a substantially larger multidimensional experimental matrix than implied by chemistry count alone. Additionally, the weak dependence of transformation temperatures on grain size, as shown in Fig.  8  and Table  4 , suggests that compositional and kinetic effects dominate the transformation behavior within the investigated processing window.

Consequently, the proposed equations should be interpreted as composition- and process-calibrated predictive relationships for CA6NM cast martensitic stainless steels within the investigated compositional and thermal processing space. Extension beyond these bounds would require further validation using independent datasets and broader chemistry ranges.

By integrating the combined effects of alloy chemistry and heating rates, the model proposed in this study establishes a quantitative framework for more accurate determination of critical transformation temperatures in cast martensitic stainless steels where existing empirical models and equilibrium-based thermodynamic calculations show substantial deviations. It improves the optimization of heat treatment parameters for cast martensitic stainless steels. A follow-up work on detailed analysis of the transformation kinetics of CA6NM is underway by the same authors to improve the understanding of the roles of key parameters in the heat treatment of CA6NM.
